t: the commandment of the red heifer. With whose ashes one who is impure from a corpse is purified (Numbers chapter 19).
and if she was old. Over four years.
lest she blacken and be disqualified. As below, halachah 2.
and they do not buy a heifer. They do not purchase it when it is younger than this age.
they fix a price for it, etc.. They set its price, but do not pay until it grows.

from the terumah of the chamber. The coins set aside in three boxes from the half-shekel funds placed in the chamber in the Temple (see Hilchot Shekalim 2:4), with which public offerings are purchased, including the red heifer (ibid. 4:1).
this is what is said in the Torah: perfect. That this does not mean free of blemish, since it is explicitly written of it "in which there is no blemish."
perfect in redness. That it be entirely red.
a dwarf was valid like other sacrificial animals. For a dwarf is disqualified in a person serving in the Temple but not in an animal (see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 8:14).
in a single hole. That grow together from one root in the skin.
cups. A cup is a cluster of adjacent hairs (like a curl).
and they prove each other. For although the hairs grow in separate cups, they are adjacent and aligned opposite each other.
their root. The place where the hairs grow.

and he is not concerned about shearing of sacred animals. For the law of the heifer is like that of consecrated property for Temple upkeep, for which the prohibition of shearing is rabbinic (see Hilchot Me'ilah 1:12), and in this case they permitted it.
and it must remain. After he cut off the black part of the hair.
so that it can be removed with tweezers. That it be long enough to be taken by scissors (R. Y. Kafah explained, based on Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 4:4, that it refers to tweezers).
it is as if it were not. If the reddish base is less than enough to be taken with tweezers, it is considered as if the hair were entirely black or white, and removing it does not help.
its hooves. The horny part that covers the ends of the toes.
he cuts off. He will cut off the black part.
a wart. A wart.

even though red hair grew in its place, it is invalid. Since it is not perfect in redness (see Raavad and commentators; and in Mishnah Achronah (Parah 2:2) and Aruch HaShulchan (53:22) they wrote that the disqualification is due to a blemish).
all the blemishes that disqualify sacrificial animals. From being offered on the altar (for the list of blemishes see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash chapter 7 and Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach chapter 2).
one born by caesarean. An offspring taken out through the wall of the abdomen and not through the womb (a caesarean section).
mechir. That was exchanged for a dog (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 4:16-18).
etnan. That was given to a prostitute as her pay (see ibid. halachot 8-15).
a treifah. An injured animal that is likely to die soon (for the definition of this term see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:6-9).
that was mounted. A person had relations with it, and these things disqualify other sacrificial animals from being offered on the altar (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:4, 3:6-7).
even though it is like consecrated property for Temple upkeep. For it is not offered on the altar, and consecrated property for Temple upkeep is not disqualified by these things.
since Scripture called it a sin offering. Scripture calls the heifer "a sin offering," and from this it is learned that for certain laws the heifer has the law of an offering (see also below 2:3).
for he does not damage his animal. Since mating might harm it (and the same is the law for other offerings, see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:15).
for work disqualifies it. If he used it for any work, it is disqualified.

and in the heifer whose neck is broken, etc.. When a slain person is found and it is not known who struck him, the city nearest the slain person is commanded to bring a heifer and break its neck (see Hilchot Rotzeach chapters 9-10). And from the verse "which has not been worked" it is learned that work disqualifies this heifer (ibid. 10:3-4).
he did other work as with a yoke. For it is written "which has not been worked."
he brought it in to thresh. To the place where grain is threshed.
he hung onto its tail and crossed the river with it. He used it for help in crossing the river.
he folded the rope over it. The rope with which he pulls the animal, and placed it on its back.
a covering of sacks. A sort of belt tied around an animal for carrying sacks and loads.
if it was rebellious. And he feared it might run away.
for any guarding that does not require a burden is a burden. Compare Hilchot Shabbat 20:8.
for another purpose it is invalid. Because of the yoke.
if by his will. The owner's will.
which has not been worked. From the passive form "worked" it is learned that even if the work was done by itself, it is disqualified as long as it was done by the owners' will.
therefore if a bird rested on it it is valid, etc.. For the owners have no benefit from this. But from a male animal they do have benefit, since it can become pregnant and give birth.
he brought it into a herd. A place where cattle are gathered, for example where they were there for threshing grain.
and it threshed by itself, it is valid. Since the threshing was not by his will.

he brought it in so that it would nurse and thresh. For example, if its mother was threshing and he brought the daughter there to nurse, and he also intended that she thresh (see also Hilchot Chovel U'Mazik 7:5).
a heifer in which a blemish was born. After they had consecrated it.
it is redeemed. They desacralize it into coins of its value and it goes out to ordinary status.

it is redeemed for its hide, etc.. Just as sacrificial animals of the altar are not redeemed so that their flesh may be fed to dogs (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:10), so the heifer is not redeemed for this purpose but only for the use of its hide.
and it does not atone. It is not fit for making sin offering ashes from it.
it was slaughtered on top of its pyre. In the place designated for it (see below 3:1-2).
it has no redemption ever. For it is a disgrace to take it out to ordinary status after they have treated it with all the procedures required in its slaughter.
it is redeemed without a blemish. Unlike sacrificial animals of the altar, which are redeemed only with a blemish.
and by oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
this one is done by Elazar. Who was the deputy of the high priest, but for all other heifers it makes no difference by which priest it is done.
four garments. The four garments of an ordinary priest (for their details see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 8:1).

who were tevul yom. Who became impure with a primary source of impurity and have already immersed but the evening has not yet come, and for certain matters they are still considered impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:1).
for their sun had not yet set. The evening after their immersion had not yet come.
pure for second tithe. For second tithe is eaten in purity and a tevul yom is valid for it (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:4).
the Sadducees. People who challenge the tradition and authority of the Sages of the Oral Torah (see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:8, Hilchot Mamrim 3:3).
with those whose sun had set. And not with tevulei yom.
by a creeping creature or the like. One of the primary sources of impurity.
all the vessels into which the ashes of the heifer are put. Which must be pure (below 13:1).
one who cuts a tube of cane. Empties the inside of the reed and makes it into a container vessel that can become impure.
he renders it impure and immerses it. In order to nullify the words of the Sadducees, as in the previous halachah.

it requires immersion because they treated it like one impure from a corpse, etc.. A rabbinic decree that a tube made for sin offering ashes is treated as impure from a corpse and renders impure the one who makes it and the one who immerses it.
like one impure from a corpse on his seventh day. After the sprinkling was done on him on the third and seventh and he requires only immersion (see below 11:1-2).

but he renders it impure in order to show the Sadducees. Although they treated it as impure from a corpse, since this is impurity only by rabbinic decree, it is no demonstration to the Sadducees, and he must render it impure again to nullify the words of the Sadducees.
valid with tevulei yom. Above 1:13-14.
just as they separate the high priest for the service of Yom Kippur. See Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:3.
and he is impure for seven days. Like anyone who has relations with a niddah (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 3:1-3).

the chamber in which he sat all seven days was the northeast one. It seems that this refers to the high priest's chamber, which was also called the Wood Chamber and the Parhedrin Chamber (see Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:3 and the commentary there).

to remind him that this is like a sin offering that is slaughtered in the north. For the red heifer is like an offering for several laws since Scripture called it a sin offering (see above 1:7), and a sin offering is slaughtered on the north side (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:2-3).
even though it is slaughtered outside. Below 3:2.
sin offering water. Living water into which the ashes of a red heifer were put and which was properly prepared to purify one impure from a corpse (and its laws are explained below, chapters 6-10).
because it is impossible for him not to be on the third day of his impurity. For three days earlier he was already in the chamber in the Temple and could not have become impure.

and by law he would need sprinkling only on the third and seventh from the separation. For the law of one impure from a corpse is that sprinkling is done on him on the third day and the seventh day from when he became impure or from when he came to be purified (below 11:1-2; and compare Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:4).
on the fourth day of the week. On Wednesday.
for sprinkling does not override Shabbat. For this is like an act of repair, which is forbidden on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 23:8, and see Hilchot Korban Pesach 6:6).
and the fourth does not need sprinkling. As explained in the previous halachah.

they sprinkle on him from the ashes of a heifer, a different heifer each day, from those that were already burned. Each day they sprinkle from the ashes of a different heifer from among those burned in the past (see below, end of chapter 3).
they sprinkle on him from it all six. All the days except the fourth day, as above halachah 4.
for the sprinkler must be pure. Below 13:1.
and likewise the vessels with which they fill and sanctify. The vessels in which they draw the living water and put the ashes of the heifer into it.
built on the rock. A natural rock under which it is unlikely that a corpse was buried.

underneath them is hollow. That beneath the courtyards there is a hollow space of at least a handbreadth in height, so that even if a corpse is buried under the rock after all, its impurity does not break through and rise to the sky but is stopped in the hollow air (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 7:5).
a grave of the deep. This is what a grave is called that is not known to anyone at all.

they bring bulls because their bellies are swollen. So that the children's feet will not hang in the air and there will be no concern that they overshadow a corpse on the way (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 3:2).
and they place doors on their backs, etc.. And the doors create a tent that separates between the children and impurity that may be beneath them.
And they go as far as the Shiloach. The Shiloach stream at the foot of the Temple Mount.
For the whole Temple Mount and the courtyards beneath them were hollow because of the grave of the depths. Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:1.
A flask of ashes. A jar containing the ashes of the red heifer.
And they would immerse the children. Because of an extra stringency they instituted regarding the purity of the sin offering (see below 13:1).
And on the Mount of Anointing. This is the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem.
And a ramp. A sloping, level surface.

And beneath it was built arches upon arches etc.. The ramp was built on two levels of arches, constructed so that the two legs of each arch on the upper level stood on the roof of two arches on the lower level. In this way there was everywhere a hollow space separating and interposing between impurity in the ground and the ramp (see also Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:1).
The place of its burning. The place prepared for burning the heifer, where it was also slaughtered.
The assistants. Those who help.
And they render the kohen impure. To nullify the words of the Sadducees (above 1:14).
My lord. Sir, a term of respect (see also Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:9).
Pines. Pine wood.
And smooth fig wood. That has no knots.
And they make a pile like a tower. They arrange the wood of the fire in a structure wide at the bottom and narrow at the top.
And they open windows in it so that the fire will be fanned through them. They create gaps between the logs of the pile so that the wind enters between them and fans the fire.
And the appearance of the pile is to the west. The front of the pile, from which the fire is lit, faces west toward the Sanctuary (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 3:8).
A reed. A kind of cane.
Its head to the south and its face to the west. Its head and the front of its body toward the south, and its face turned toward the west.
And the kohen stands in the east, facing west. Together with the heifer inside the pile.

And receives the blood in his left hand. In the palm of his hand and not in a vessel (see below 4:4), even though in other sacrifices service with the left hand disqualifies (see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 5:18).
Opposite the Holy of Holies. He must see the Sanctuary at the time of the sprinkling (see below 4:5).
Into the body of the heifer. So that the blood will be burned together with the heifer.
And guards. Waits.
Cedar wood and hyssop. See Numbers 19:6.
No less than a handbreadth. For the hyssop, but there is no measure for the cedar (Commentary on the Mishnah 3:9; compare Hilchot Tumat Tzara'at 11:1).
And wool dyed with crimson. Crimson worm, a kind of red dye, as explained later in the halachah.
The weight of five selaim. The weight of five coins called sela.
With pu'ah. A plant that yields a red dye that is not found today.
With lakkah. The lac insect, from which the purple dye was produced (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 9:1; see also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 8:13).
And the worm is the berries etc.. The dye with which the wool was dyed was extracted from an insect that grows on a plant and is composed of small red berries.
The og. A plant with red clusters, from which the spice sumac is made (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Dema'i 1:1).
The hyssop that householders eat and season pots with. This is also the hyssop with which the waters of the sin offering are sprinkled (below 11:5). From it the spice called za'atar is made.
The three of them are indispensable to one another. The commandment is fulfilled only with all three, and if one is missing it is invalid.
On a strip of crimson. A strip of the wool dyed with crimson worm.
Into the midst of the burning of. This implies that they are to be thrown in at the time of the burning, not before or after.
They beat it with sticks. In order to crush it into ashes.
And they sift everything in sieves. Strainers, so that fine ash comes out.
And everything black. Any black part that became charcoal.
And that has no ash in it. That was not burned enough to be made into ash.
In the chel. The wall surrounding the Temple court on the inside of the Temple Mount wall (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:3).
And one is divided among all the watches. Among the twenty-four places where they guarded the Temple (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 3:11; see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 8:4).
And seven from Ezra until the destruction of the Temple. And the names of those who made them are listed in Mishnah Parah 3:5.
As it is said, "and he shall slaughter it". And not it and another.
They do not bring out a black one with it etc.. In order to make the heifer come.
Not for its own sake. That he slaughtered it for the sake of another offering (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 13:1).
Or received or sprinkled. Its blood.
Or for its sake and not for its sake, or not for its sake and for its sake. Whether he began it for its own sake and ended not for its sake, or the reverse, it is invalid.
Or it was done by a non-kohen. For example, he received or sprinkled its blood; but the slaughter is valid by a non-kohen after the fact (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:2).
Lacking garments. A kohen who is not wearing all his priestly garments.
Or did it in golden garments. For its commandment is in the garments of an ordinary kohen (above 1:12).
He slaughtered it with intent to eat of its flesh or drink of its blood. And not to burn it as is its commandment.

It is valid, because "a pleasing aroma" was not said of it. Unlike other offerings where this expression is said, from which it is learned that when performing the offering one must think that it will be burned on the altar for the sake of God (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:11).
Its commandment is a commandment of the hand. Above 3:2.
Even one of them. One of the seven sprinklings (above, there).
His sprinkling is invalid. And he must sprinkle again seven valid sprinklings (and so below, halachah 7).
If he dipped twice and sprinkled once, his sprinkling is invalid. Because he must dip his finger in the blood once for each sprinkling (above 3:2).
Even though he did not count the second sprinkling. He did not count it among the seven sprinklings.
Because he engaged in something unneeded at the time of the burning. And work disqualifies the heifer (below, halachah 17).

If he took the blood outside its pile and sprinkled, it is invalid. For he must sprinkle inside the pile so that the blood will be burned with it (Chidushei HaRambam, Parah 3:10; Amek HaNetziv, Sifrei Chukat 124).
He sprinkled its blood at night... it is invalid. For its whole commandment is by day (below, halachah 17).

Outside the place of its burning. The special place for it on the Mount of Anointing (above 3:1), and it is invalid like an offering slaughtered outside its place (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 14:1, cited in Keren Orah, Zevachim 112a).
Even if he slaughtered it within the wall. Of Jerusalem, and although it is near the Temple site, it is invalid.
He flayed it and cut it up and then burned all of it - it is valid. Although initially it should be burned whole.
And if he left out any of it. He left some of it unburned.
Even its dung. The digested food in its intestines.
It burst from its hide etc.. It flew off because of the fire and landed outside the place of its burning.
And if he did not return it, it is invalid. Since all of it must be burned.
It burst outside its pile. Outside the tower of wood (see above 3:2) but still inside the place of its burning.
Adds to it. Wood.
From its hooves. The horny part covering the tips of its toes.
He need not return. For all these, once they have been placed on the pile, no longer prevent validity if they burst off.

It is not disqualified by being left overnight. If the night passed over it before its commandment was completed, it is not disqualified, although with sacrificial offerings, being left overnight disqualifies.
An onen. A mourner on the day of death, who nonetheless is forbidden on that day to serve in the Temple (see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 2:6).

One lacking atonement. A zav or metzora who purified from his impurity but has not yet brought his offering, and who is forbidden to enter the Temple and to eat sacred foods (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1).
Because its acts are like service. Temple service, and every kohen who serves in the Temple must wash his hands and feet first (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 5:1).
In a service vessel inside. In the courtyard, see there 5:10.
And even in an earthenware ladle. A simple clay vessel that is not fit to be a service vessel.
As we have explained. Above 1:14.
He need not return and sanctify. Although generally one who became impure must again sanctify his hands and feet (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 5:6).
Or with any wood. That is not of the woods specified above, 3:2.
With stubble. Straw and dung from the fields.
To increase the dust. For hyssop makes the ash fine and plentiful (Tosefta Parah 4:10).

This is like mixing ash of burning into the ash of the heifer. Ash of a burning that is not from the heifer; if even a little of it is mixed into the heifer's ash it disqualifies all of it, as below 9:14.
And work disqualifies it. If he engaged in something else, he disqualified it.
At the time of his entering. At the time he gathered the ash.
From a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor. Who lack understanding.
From the tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
That his eyes be on it. And not on something else.

To teach that work disqualifies it from the time of slaughter until it is made into ash. Since we learned from what is said regarding slaughter and burning that work disqualifies in them, we say that the law applies from the time of slaughter until it becomes ash.
And another animal was slaughtered with it, or a gourd was cut with it. Unintentionally.
For the slaughter of unconsecrated animals does not require intention. Hilchot Shechitah 2:11.
They defile garments for the whole time of their preparation. As explained below, halachah 2.
And they require immersion and nightfall by Torah law. Like anyone who became impure with a primary source of impurity (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:1).
The one who guards it at the time of its preparation. The one who guards it from its slaughter until its ashes are gathered (for the reason for the guarding see Aruch HaShulchan 60:6).
Lest he move a limb of it. And become impure by Torah law, like all who deal with the heifer.

For any garment or vessel the impure person touches... they are impure. And they become a first degree of impurity, as follows. But if he touched foods and liquids, they become a second degree (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 6:15), and if he touched a person or an earthenware vessel, they are not impure at all (Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav UMoshav 6:2).
One who carries a carcass. It is a primary source of impurity, and the person carrying it defiles his clothes (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 1:1).

And they are a first degree of impurity. Even though they did not touch the carcass directly, they become a first degree of impurity because they touched a person while he himself was touching the carcass (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 1:2).
A derivative of impurity. A first degree of impurity and those below it.
For a derivative of impurity does not defile vessels. Only foods and liquids.
As we have explained at the beginning of the book. Hilchot Tumat Met 5:7.
And likewise anything similar to a carcass. Any impurity where the one who touches or carries it defiles clothes has the law written here.
And the heifer itself does not defile a person or vessels that touched it. As long as they have not been engaged with it.
In dividing the ash or in storing it. See above 3:4.
The sin offerings that are burned. Sin offerings whose flesh is burned outside the Temple (unlike ordinary sin offerings whose flesh is eaten by the kohanim).

Of the bulls. The bull brought by the High Priest on Yom Kippur, and the bull for a matter hidden from the community, and the bull that comes for all the commandments (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:15-16).
And of the goats. The Yom Kippur goat whose blood is brought inside, and the goats of idolatry (there).
From the tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
A binyan av. A halachic source that serves as a basis for other laws derived from it.
In the Beit HaDeshen. A place outside Jerusalem where the burned sin offerings are burned (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:4).
But if they became disqualified in the courtyard, they are burned there, like disqualified sacrificial offerings. There, halachah 3.
The scapegoat. The live goat sent to the wilderness on Yom Kippur (see Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 3:7).
And some of the carriers went out. That only the front carriers went out.
And the last ones. The rear ones.
Went out. The bulls or goats.
The one who carries them in the courtyard. Who is not one of those who took them outside earlier.
He was standing outside the courtyard. A pure person.
And pulls them from there. Those bulls and goats that went out and returned.
The water on which the ash of the heifer is put. In order to sanctify them for the purification of one impure through a corpse (as explained below, chapter 11).
Or from rivers that draw from them. That are drawn from springs.
Living water. Spring water (as opposed to rainwater). This water is also used for the purification of the zav and for the birds of the metzora (Hilchot Mikva'ot 9:8).
This is called sanctification. The manner of sanctification and its laws will be explained below in chapter 9.
Waters of niddah. From the root "yadah," meaning throwing, i.e., water used for sprinkling.
Except for a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor. Like the law of gathering the ash (above 4:17).
And they do not sprinkle. On the impure person.
And they do not dip. The bundle of hyssop in the waters of the sin offering in order to sprinkle from it on the impure person.
They do not sprinkle or dip except by day. Below 11:1.
Even in vessels of dung, vessels of stone, and vessels of earth. Although they do not receive impurity, they are considered vessels for the waters of the sin offering.
And in a ship. Although it is not considered a vessel regarding receiving impurity (Hilchot Kelim 18:9).
In the sides of vessels. Sides broken off from vessels that have a receptacle.
In the bottoms of the machatz. A deep earthenware base in which vessels are placed.
In the stopper of a barrel. The lid of a barrel. All these vessels were not originally intended to be receptacles (see Hilchot Berachot 6:11).
In his hollowed hands. In the palms of his hands.
In a hen's egg. The eggshell after he emptied it of its contents.
And not in the trough in the rock. A hollow carved in a rock attached to the ground. None of these are vessels (see there, Hilchot Mikva'ot 6:3).
The potters' egg. A ball of clay from which the potter makes a vessel (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 5:6).
Until he planes them. Smooths them.
And an ostrich egg. The egg of an ostrich, which receives impurity when it has been plated (see Hilchot Kelim 1:2).
Even if he attached it with plaster. Although the plaster attaches the vessel firmly to the ground, it does not lose its status as a vessel.
He made a crown of clay around the vessel. A rim at its mouth.

It is as if he made a crown of clay around the rock or on the ground. Since the crown is not properly attached to the vessel, it is not considered a vessel, and its law is that of a crown attached to the ground.
That was pierced with a hole that admits liquid. That has a hole of such a size that, if the vessel is placed in liquids, they enter the vessel through this hole.
Pierced with a hole that lets liquid out. That if the vessel is filled with liquids, they drip out through its hole; this is a smaller hole than one that admits liquid (see also Hilchot Kelim 19:2).
They are not on the roundness of the vessel. They do not rest on the whole bottom of the vessel because of the rags.
One who sprays water from the spring. Splashes the spring's water into the barrel.
Or vegetable leaves. That are fit for eating and receive impurity.
Reed leaves and walnut leaves. That do not receive impurity.
The pit. A cistern.
Like a mikveh and not like a spring. It is not considered living water.
And all the rivers. That do not draw from springs but from other sources such as snow.
That are dragged along. That flow (see also Hilchot Mikva'ot 9:12-13).
The salty ones. The same applies to bitter water, which is considered like water that has been struck (Hilchot Mikva'ot 9:7).
The lukewarm ones. Slightly warm.
They draw out. They remove water from its source.
And a spring that first emerged. A new spring.
Waters of swamps. Marsh waters.
And the waters of the Yarmuch. A stream on the eastern side of the Jordan.
For they are mixed waters. Mixed with water that is not living water.
On their own. Naturally.
A flow of rainwater fell into it. And changed the appearance of the water.
Until it clears. Until it returns to being clear as it was.
An aqueduct coming from afar. A channel whose spring is far from here.
And he is found filling from water whose beginning was cut off from the spring. And it is no longer living water.
Before they are sanctified. Before he puts the ash of the heifer on them and they become sanctified water.
Words of tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
Or at the time he pours them from vessel to vessel. See below 10:1.
Like cave water. Which is invalid for the sin offering since it is not living water.
Like ash of burning. Ash of a burning not from the heifer, which is invalid for the sin offering.

And he gives him his wages as an idle worker. They assess how much a person would want to be paid not to do the work he is engaged in and earns from, and to do instead such light work whose pay is small, and pay him accordingly. This depends on the heaviness of his work and the amount of its pay (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 4:6).
With an impurity that prevents him from eating his terumah. For an impure kohen may not eat terumah (Hilchot Terumot 7:1), nor anoint with terumah oil, for anointing is like drinking (there 11:1).
He feeds him, gives him drink, and anoints him. In place of the terumah that he prevented him from eating and anointing with.
With one hand. With a single hand.
And we have already informed that work disqualifies the filling. Above, halachah 1.
One who fills for others... all are valid. Water that was properly filled for others, and then the filler did work before putting in the ash, is valid (below 8:5).
For it is all one filling. And it is considered as if he drew once.
And only the last is valid. Since he did no work after he filled it.
And they changed their minds. They regretted and changed their minds.
For the filler did not engage in another filling. Each of the fillers was engaged in only one filling and did no other work until it was sanctified.

Even though he returned and changed his mind... only the last is valid. Since at the time of filling his intention was for five sanctifications, and each of the barrels was already disqualified by the filling of the barrel after it.

He filled them to sanctify them in one sanctification... only the one he sanctified first is valid. And the rest of the water in the barrels is invalid because the sanctification of the first barrel counts as work and disqualifies the water in the other barrels (Rash and Rosh, Parah 7:1).
Only the one of them that was sanctified first is valid. For once he said "sanctify for you," the water entered the domain of his fellow and has the law of the filler (see below 8:2).

Then all of them are valid. For once he said "sanctify for me," his fellow does not enter in his place and the water was not disqualified either by the filling or by the sanctification, as he explains.
For he did not sanctify; another sanctified for him. And his fellow does not disqualify water that is not his (see below 8:3).
And he places them before him and goes. But he may not place the water he wishes to sanctify behind him, as explained below 10:4.
And they lifted it one upon the other. They helped each other to lift the barrel onto the shoulder.
If both filled for one sanctification, the water is valid. Because these actions are among the needs of filling, and both are filling for the same sanctification.
The one who lifted or removed the thorn disqualified his water. For he did work not needed for his own filling.
To fill with it. To hang the bucket on it in order to draw water.
On his way. He need not leave his path to reach it.
While walking. As he walks, without stopping (see below 8:1).
He disqualified the water. For walking not needed is considered work.
He disqualified the water. Because of work.
And if he was drawing and gathering into his hand etc.. That he wraps the rope around his hand as he raises the bucket.
One who fills and puts into the barrel until he fills it with water. He fills water in a small vessel and pours it into the barrel, and does so several times until the barrel is full.
And stored the barrel so that it would not break while he was filling. During his engagement in filling, he moved the barrel to a protected place.

Or turned it upside down in order to dry it and fill it. After he filled the water in the small vessel, he turned the barrel over so that it would dry and he could put water for the sin offering in it (see below 9:8).
To carry the sanctified in it. The heifer's ash or the water after they were sanctified.
And puts into the trough. That is not attached to the ground.
So that the potsherds should not hinder him when he pours the water. That they not interfere when he wants to transfer the water to another vessel.
If before the bucket reached the water he intended. To fill it for the waters of the sin offering.

He pours out and need not dry. He pours out the water that filled the bucket, since the one filling the water must intend for the sin offering (below 9:2), and since his initial intention was to drink the water, it is not valid for the sin offering. But since the filling itself was done for the sin offering, the water does not have the law of water unfit for sanctification that requires drying (see below 9:9; Kesef Mishneh).
He pours out and must dry. Since the water was not filled for the sin offering, it is unfit for sanctification and requires drying.
He lowered the bucket. With intent to drink.
And the rope broke from his hand. And he changed his mind and intended it for the waters of the sin offering.

While it was still in the water he intended it for the waters of the sin offering - he pours out and need not dry. The commentators found this clause difficult to explain and most emended here to read: "he pours out and must dry," with the same meaning as in the first clause (Kesef Mishneh and others; see Mirkevet HaMishneh and Rambam LaAm, who maintained the text as is).
He disqualified the water. For tilting the vessel is considered work that disqualifies the water.
Or that she performed chalitzah before him. That he served as one of the judges before whom chalitzah is performed (see Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 4:5).
Or performed refusal. A girl who refuses is a minor orphan who was betrothed and refuses to remain with her husband (Hilchot Ishut 4:7-8); the refusal is done before two (see Hilchot Gerushin 11:8).
For he engaged in something else. That is not needed for transporting the water.
While walking. As he walks, without stopping.
Or killed a snake or scorpion that hinders him. As he walks.
This is the rule: a matter that is considered work. That is, that disqualifies because of work, since it is not needed for transporting the water.

And a matter that is not considered work. That does not disqualify as work, since it is needed for transporting the water. Even so, if he stopped he disqualified, since he could have done it without stopping (see Mishnah Acharonah, Parah 7:9).
He was walking in the water. That is, while carrying the water for the sin offering.
And broke through. Opened a path for himself.
In order to fence. Afterward.
Valid. Since he did not stop and the act he performed was needed for transporting the water, whereas the thought he thought does not disqualify.
And likewise if he cut fruit to eat. As he walked.
To set aside the rest. To spread what remains for him to dry.
The drying place. A place designated for drying fruit.
The water is valid. Because he did no work and did not even stop.
The sanctifier. The one who puts the ash of the heifer on the water.

For work does not disqualify the sanctification, only the water etc.. The act of sanctifying is not itself disqualified by work; rather, the water filled for the sin offering is disqualified by work as long as it was not sanctified. And since the work disqualification is only through the owner or guardian of the water, the water is not disqualified by the work of the person who sanctified.
One who sanctifies for himself and another at once. In two different vessels.
With both hands at once. That he fills two vessels together, one vessel in each hand.

For one sanctification it is invalid; for two sanctifications it is valid. The commentators found the explanation difficult according to our text, and some emended: "for one sanctification it is valid; for two sanctifications it is invalid" (Ohr Sameach and Be'er Avraham, based on Kesef Mishneh). According to this, when he fills for one sanctification the two acts of filling count as one filling and therefore do not disqualify because of work (see above 7:4). But when he fills for two sanctifications each filling disqualifies the other because of work (see above 7:3; see Mirkevet HaMishneh, Aruch HaShulchan, and Chidushei HaRambam on Tosefta Parah 6:5, who explained the Rambam according to our text).
With both hands as one. He holds a little ash in each hand and drops it onto the water at once.
For one sanctification. That he put all the ash into the same vessel.
For two sanctifications they are invalid. For each of the sanctifications disqualifies the water in the other vessel because of work.
He filled and sanctified with both hands at once for himself - both are invalid. For each of the acts disqualifies the water in the other vessel because of work.
Both are valid. Like the law of one who sanctifies for two at once (above, halachah 4).
The filling is invalid and the sanctification is valid. For work disqualifies in the filling but not in the sanctification.
And anything in his hand, and he did work etc.. Since he holds the water in his hand, he disqualifies it through work even though there is another guardian there.
For he sanctified for a fee. And sanctification for a fee disqualifies, as above 7:2.
In exchange for this filling. In return for this filling.
And he does not intend another filling. For his fellow already filled for him.
For work does not disqualify the sanctification. Therefore the sanctification is valid even though the act of sanctifying was done with the intention that his fellow fill for him.
For it is like one filling and sanctifying at once. Since he fills in exchange for the sanctification.
And valid. For all these are needed for the sanctification.

He tilted the vessel containing the ash in his hand so that it would not scatter. After pouring a little of the ash from the vessel into his hand to sanctify the water with it, he tilted it back and held it upright in his hand so that the ash would not spill excessively.
Because it is impossible etc.. For this is the only way to keep the ash from scattering without disqualifying the water.
And took from it to sanctify other water - valid. And only from the floating ash that did not touch the water (see below 9:3).
Nipped. Cut.
To scoop the ash with it. To collect the ash with it from the vessel in which it is found.
If so that he not hold much ash. So that too much ash not be poured into the water; since this is not among the needs of filling, it disqualifies the water.
And if so that the ash enter the vessel. The vessel in which the water is, so that it not spill outside it; in this case the nipping of the leaf is among the needs of filling.
So that it is visible on the surface of the water. So that it not be absorbed in it at once but remain a while on the surface of the water.
Even if it is a large barrel full of water. No more than this amount is needed.
And what is this that is said in the Torah, "and he shall put on it living water"?. Which apparently implies that the water is put on the ash.
In order to mix the ash with the water. And then it will float on it.

"And they shall take for the impure". From this, the taking of the ash and putting it on the water must be for the purification of the impure. From this verse they also learned that the sanctifier himself must be the one who joins the water and ash (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 6:1).
And for the sprinkling. See below 10:7.
But if it fell. Unintentionally.
Or he took the ash in his hand and his fellow pushed him etc.. Although he took the ash intentionally, the act of putting it in the water was not intentional.
Or the ash fell from his hand on the side of the vessel... it is invalid. In these cases the sanctification is invalid because the ash did not reach the water directly from the sanctifier's hands.
Less than enough for sprinkling. The amount needed to dip the tops of the hyssop in the water (below 15:1).
And even if the wind blew etc.. Although there is no valid sanctification here, the ash is not fit for another sanctification.
Because they are not in the vessel. And one sanctifies only in a vessel (above 6:2).
Sprinkles. Pours into another vessel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 6:3, Rashi, Yoma 58a). Some explain: sprinkles the waters of the sin offering (Rash, Parah there).
And he shall not touch the sponge. For if he touches it, water will be squeezed out of it.
Even though the water floats on top of it, however little. And therefore it is possible that no water came out of the sponge.
And they mix with the valid water. And disqualify even in the smallest amount (below, halachah 8).

If a sponge fell into the sanctified water, he takes it and squeezes it outside the vessel. Although the water was sanctified before it was absorbed by the sponge, they decreed not to squeeze it inside the vessel because of the case where it was absorbed before being sanctified (Kesef Mishneh in the name of Rabbi Yosef Korkos; see there for further explanations).
Two troughs of stone. Not attached to the ground.

Like the tube of a skin bottle. A hollow reed placed in the mouth of a leather bottle for drinking and the like (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 5:8; its measure is the diameter of two average fingers: Hilchot Mikva'ot 8:6).
The water in the second is sanctified. In these ways the water in the two vessels is considered connected.

Two stones that he surrounded one with the other etc.. It seems the case here is where each part is a receptacle standing by itself, and he inserted one into the other so that both became one receptacle, and joined them firmly so that the water does not leak out. When the joining is not strong, so that if one part is lifted it separates from the other, only the water in the vessel in which the ash was put is sanctified, while the water between them and the water in the other part are not sanctified (and they do not disqualify the water in the sanctified part even though all the water is mixed - Mirkevet HaMishneh; see Rash and Rosh, Parah 5:9, who explained the case such that only the water between them is not sanctified but the rest of the water is sanctified).
With gypsum. Plaster.
And he must dry the vessel. So that nothing remain there that would disqualify the water.
Komos and kalkantos. Kinds of dyes.
Marks. Dyes.

One who immerses a vessel for the sin offering. For example, if it was impure (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 5:2), or because of the stringencies the Sages instituted regarding the purity of the sin offering (below 13:1).
In water not fit for sanctification. That is not living water.

He need not dry. Although the waters of the sin offering require intention for filling (above, halachah 2), since the immersion of the vessel was done for the sin offering, this water is not so disqualified as to require drying afterward (see further above 7:11 and the commentary there).
To gather sanctified water in it. To put in it water that was already sanctified.
Either way he must dry. For sanctified water is disqualified by any mixture, even of water fit for sanctification.
A gourd. A gourd that is emptied and becomes like a wooden vessel.

That they immersed in water fit for sanctification. That they drew spring water with it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 5:3; other commentators explained that they immersed it in it for the purity of the sin offering, as where it was pure beforehand but not for the sake of the sin offering).
One may sanctify in it. It is permitted afterward to fill it with living water with intent to fill and sanctify it, for in this matter we are not concerned with the small amount of water it absorbed.
Because the water in which it was immersed is absorbed in it etc.. Therefore even if he dried it beforehand, this does not help.
They will come out and mix with the water that they sanctify in it. And they will defile it and disqualify it.

Or their appearance changed. The appearance of the water (Kesef Mishneh, Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 9:2). Some explain that this refers to the appearance of the creeping creatures (Rash MiShantz there, who wrote that the Rambam retracted his words in the Commentary on the Mishnah; see further in the halachah).
Invalid. Because of the fluid emitted by the creeping creatures that mixes with the water.
And the dira and kinnah in grain. Kinds of insects found in grain.

And its appearance did not change. The Kesef Mishneh explained this as referring to the appearance of the water and therefore emended here: "and their appearance did not change," whereas in the opinion of the Rash MiShantz no emendation is needed and it refers to the appearance of the beetle.
Because it is like a tube. For it is hollow.
Invalid. Because of the saliva coming out of their mouths and mixing with the water.
On their own. Naturally and not because of something mixed into them.
Because of smoke they are invalid. And the same applies if they changed because of anything else.
They congealed. They froze.
And they melted. They thawed.
But if he melted them with fire they are invalid. For they changed not on their own.
Because of smoke it is valid. For it is crushed immediately after the burning (see above 3:3), while it is still giving off smoke (see Chidushei HaRambam, Tosefta Parah 9:7).
Ash of burning. Ash of a burning that is not from the heifer.

They are not disqualified until it drinks from them. Then it disqualifies them because of the saliva in its mouth, like other domestic and wild animals (for a similar case regarding water that was not sanctified see above 7:11).
Lest a person not pure for the sin offering touched them. And disqualified them by his touch.
If the weasel can drink from it. The same applies to other domestic animals, wild animals, or creeping creatures that disqualify by drinking.
And if not. That they have no way to drink from the water, even though they may have removed the vessel's cover.
Or domestic animal, wild animal, or creeping creature. That although they disqualify by drinking, they do not disqualify by touch (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 11:1).
These are invalid. Because they are in the domain of the impure person (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 7:10; see below 14:4).
Two who were guarding etc.. See above 8:2.
And he leaves them with him unsanctified as long as he wishes and this is nothing. As long as he does no work that disqualifies the water.

And the water became impure. Because it was in a place that is not pure (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 9:6; see below 14:1-3). Some explain that it became impure with corpse impurity because they overshadowed the corpse (Rashi, Chagigah 23a, Yevamot 116b).

And he shall not float them on the surface of the water. He shall not transport them in a vessel floating on the water or by swimming while holding in his hand the vessel with the waters of the sin offering or the ash, for all these are similar to transport by ship.
If he filled two barrels. For waters of the sin offering, in a way that they are not disqualified because of work.
Because he weighed them on a scale. To know how much they weigh.
He diverted his attention. He removed his thought from guarding them.
But if he weighed other things with the waters of the sin offering. That he knew their weight and used them to weigh other things.
Those who immersed that day. Who became impure with a primary source of impurity and already immersed, but nightfall has not yet come.
As we have explained. Above 1:13.
And because of the Sadducees etc.. See there, halachah 14.
Vessels of flow. Vessels that have purification in a mikveh (excluding earthenware vessels).
And a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it is not apparent whether he is male or female. [Note: In the Commentary on the Mishnah the Rambam vocalizes this word "tumtom."]
And an androginos. One who has both male and female sexual organs.

For an uncircumcised person is not impure. Although for other laws an uncircumcised person is considered impure more severely than one who immersed that day (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:4), regarding sprinkling he is not considered impure.
The sprinkler must intend. See above 9:2.
He need not immerse. To dip the hyssop in the water.
Until the water is finished. The water on the hyssop.
The dripping water. That drips from the hyssop.
Even the tops of stalks. For this is the measure of sprinkling (below 15:1).
Provided that he not absorb. That he not wipe the sides or walls of the vessel with the hyssop.

And he need not be careful lest he touch the sides of the vessel a second time. We do not worry that perhaps the water on the hyssop is not from the dipping but from absorbing the sides of the vessel.
Stalks. Hard woody branches growing from the root of the plant.
And in each strand one stalk. In each of the three branches at least one green stalk grows.
On the third day and on the seventh day. Of their impurity.
Immerses. The one purifying.
And waits for nightfall. Waits until evening.
And the water defiles as waters of the sin offering. Like all waters of the sin offering, which defile one who touches or carries them unnecessarily (below 15:1).
As will be explained. There.
As we have explained. In the previous paragraph.
An am ha'aretz... is not believed lest he became impure today. Because he is not expert and careful in the laws of impurity and purity (see Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav UMoshav 10:1).
A chaver. A person who accepted upon himself to be careful regarding impurity and purity (there).
And eats sacred foods in the evening. For as long as he was uncircumcised he was forbidden sacred foods (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:9).
The commandment of hyssop. Ideally.
And its remainders are two. If one of them fell off later and only two remained, it is valid.
And if he took two at first and bound them, it is valid. After the fact.
The stalks separated. Their binding was loosened (Mirkevet HaMishneh), but the stalks are still in his hand.
Even if of each stalk only a little remained. Almost all the leaves fell off the stalks.
And the remainders of the hyssop any amount. If it broke and became shorter, it is valid as long as any measure remains.
A stalk with three strands in it. Three stalks come out of the root.
Separates them. Cuts them from the root and separates them.
Valid. After the fact.
The short hyssop. That does not reach the waters of the sin offering at the bottom of the vessel.
The spindle. A wooden implement used for spinning.
Not with the young shoots of hyssop. This is the early stage of the hyssop's growth before it puts out leaves.
And not with the pods. At the end of the hyssop's growth, after it put out pod-like structures at its top containing the seeds (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 11:7).
Only with stalks. After the hyssop grew a little and put out leaves.
Stalks that have not ripened. That have not put out leaves.
From when it sprouts. From when it finishes putting out its buds.
To purify the metzora with it. To sprinkle with it on the metzora to purify him from his tzara'at (see Hilchot Tumat Tzara'at 11:1).
By itself. Without an added name.
Ezov-yon and kochalit hyssop etc.. Kinds of hyssop that have a qualifying name.
Asherah. A tree planted to serve as idolatry.
A condemned city. A city most of whose inhabitants worshiped idols and all of whose property must be burned (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah, chapter 4).

And of idolatry. Property belonging to idolatry. All of these, since they are destined for destruction, are not valid for sprinkling (see also Hilchot Tzitzit 1:11, Hilchot Shofar 1:3, Hilchot Lulav 8:1).
And of impure terumah. Whose law is that of any impure hyssop, which is invalid for sprinkling (below 15:9).
And of pure terumah he shall not sprinkle. Ideally, because it may cause loss as a result.
That he gathered for wood. For heating and the like, and therefore it does not receive impurity, since it is not designated as human food (see Hilchot Tumat Okhalin 1:1).
Dries it. So that invalid water not mix with valid.
He gathered it for food. For eating.
And liquids fell on it. One of the seven liquids that make food susceptible to impurity (see there, halachah 2).
As will be explained. Below 13:1.

Even though the tongue is like the exposed limbs regarding impurity, as we have explained etc.. Although regarding receiving impurity the tongue is considered an external limb, so that if impurity touches it the person becomes impure (Hilchot Tumat Met 1:3), regarding becoming purified from impurity it is considered a concealed place into which water need not enter at the time of immersion (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 1:10; and see Bavli Kiddushin 25a), and likewise contact of the waters of the sin offering with it does not purify the person.
From the residue. The water that dripped on it from the first.
Vessels made of parts. That are made of several pieces.
Scissors of sections. Scissors whose parts can be taken apart.
And a rehitni chisel. The blade attached to the handle. These vessels are made so that their parts can be removed from one another when not in use.
And not at the time of work. Even if the parts are joined together.
Because they are like one vessel. See also Hilchot Kelim 13:14.
The launderers' loose-stitched garments. Garments joined to one another by temporary stitching done by launderers.
And a garment sewn with kilayim. Wool and linen together (see Hilchot Kilayim, chapter 10).
The baskets on the kantal. Baskets hung together on a carrying pole (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 12:9).
And the bed of the tarbal. A vessel made of wooden beams used for threshing grain (there).
And the horn of the klikhah. A collapsible bed, whose legs are called "keren" (there).
And horns of travelers. Vessels that wayfarers use for drinking.
And a chain of keys. A bunch of keys. All these are vessels made so that they can be taken apart and separated from one another.
Moreover etc.. When they are more numerous than these measures, they are not considered one vessel.
The cover of the boiler etc.. A water boiler whose lid is attached to it by a chain (and this lid receives impurity, see Hilchot Kelim 9:6).
The bell and its clapper. The bell and the clapper that strikes it (for their impurity see Hilchot Kelim 8:8).
The spindle with which they spin etc.. A spinning implement (spindle) used for spinning flax threads or for twisting ropes made of papyrus (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 12:9).
The wood around which the spun thread is wrapped. On which the spun thread is wound.
With which they twist and spin. Through which the spinning itself is done.

And the whorl in the middle of the spindle. A sort of half-sphere attached to the spindle to weigh it down during spinning so that the spun thread is properly stretched (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 11:6).
Only on the tzenirah. Because it is the main part of the vessel.
And of flax. The spindle intended for spinning flax, whose parts are firmly joined (there).
A leather cradle sheet that is attached to the buttons. A leather sheet spread beneath a baby in the bed to keep it clean (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 26:6), and attached to it with buttons.
The malben of beds. A decorated wooden board mounted on the side of a bed for ornament (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 18:3).
Is not a connection, either for impurity or for sprinkling. But if it is attached to the bed, it is a connection to it regarding impurity (see Hilchot Kelim 4:2).
The bored ones. That have a hole into which the vessel enters.
The knife handle. The haft of the knife.
The tight-fitting ones. That have a protrusion that enters into the vessel.
Is not a connection for sprinkling. For they are not firmly attached.
Even if he immersed for sacred purposes. For eating sacred foods or for Temple service.
Until he immerses for the sake of the sin offering. See also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 13:2.

Like impure foods and liquids. That defile the waters of the sin offering (below 14:10) and one pure for the sin offering who touches them with his hands (below, halachah 10). The liquids also defile vessels that touched them (below, halachah 3).

A vessel fit for lying or sitting. That is used for lying or sitting and can become a primary source of impurity through the pressure of a zav and the like (the impurity of midras and its laws are explained in Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav UMoshav, chapters 6-7).
It is, regarding the sin offering, like the midras of a zav. And below, halachah 7, it is explained how it defiles one pure for the sin offering.
Yochanan ben Gudgeda. A sage who lived in the Temple period and was one of the Levites who served in the Temple.

He ate in the purity of sacred things all his days. He was careful to eat unconsecrated food in purity as if it were sacred food (see Hilchot Tumat Okhalin 16:12). Even so, regarding the red heifer his clothes were considered impure with the impurity of midras (see also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 13:1).
Derivatives of impurities. All impurities that are not a primary source of impurity (a first degree and those below it: see Hilchot Tumat Met 5:8).
As we have explained. There, halachah 7.
Lest liquids fall on the sandal. But if they fell on his foot, they do not defile it (below, halachah 10; for other garments they did not decree: see Kesef Mishneh and Ra'avad).
For all liquids are impure regarding the sin offering. And they defile the sandal by Rabbinic law, like all impure liquids that defile vessels (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 7:2).
And this sanctifier would become impure by touching the sandal. For every derivative of impurity defiles a person and vessels regarding the sin offering.
And the waters of the sin offering would be found impure. That they would become impure because of the sanctifying person.
One whose hands alone became impure through things that defile the hands. Various impurities that do not defile the person but only his hands (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 8:1).
For example, he touched foods or liquids. For all foods and liquids are impure regarding the sin offering (above, halachah 1).
Even though he is pure for sacred purposes. Even though this person is not defiled regarding sacred things.
As will be explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 8:7.
And he is a first degree of impurity. That defiles the sin offering like anyone requiring immersion (below, halachah 5).
Anyone requiring immersion, whether by Torah law or by Rabbinic law. A person who requires immersion, including one who is pure for sacred purposes but not pure for the sin offering.
And the one who sprinkles the waters of the sin offering. And the same applies that he defiles any person who is pure for the sin offering (Acharonim and Tiferet Yisrael, Parah 6:11).

By touch and by carrying. By touching them or carrying them (the impurity of carrying mentioned here is where the impure person carried the pure one, and it is like the impurity of shifting, in which the zav defiles the pure: see Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav UMoshav 8:2).
The prepared hyssop. On which liquids pure for the sin offering fell and made it susceptible to receive impurity.

And an impure person who touched part of the sin offering ash disqualified all of it. For example, when it is placed in a vessel, because of the stringency instituted for sacred things and the sin offering, that the vessel joins what is inside it (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 12:7, and see Tiferet Yisrael, Eduyot 8:1).
In the way that they count for terumah and sacred things. As detailed in Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot, chapter 11.

Even if only its back became impure regarding the sin offering. Even though the vessel touched pure liquids and became impure only because of the stringency of the sin offering, and even though the impurity was only on the outside of the vessel (which in unconsecrated food and terumah does not defile the whole vessel: Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 7:3, 12:2), nevertheless it becomes entirely impure and defiles the vessels that touch it.

Anything fit to become impure through the midras of a zav... became impure even though he did not touch it. For regarding the sin offering they were stringent to consider everything that receives midras impurity as if it became impure with actual midras, and therefore it defiles the person who moves it even without touching (see Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav UMoshav 7:2).

And likewise one pure for the sin offering who moved a person etc.. Since a person is fit to become impure with zivah, they were stringent that he defiles one pure for the sin offering who moves him, or his spittle or urine, even if he did not touch them (see there 1:1, 1:14).
A vessel defiled by a corpse. Which is not fit to become impure by midras.
As we have explained. Hilchot Tumat Met 5:9.
And likewise if he shifted a creeping creature or semen. Which are among the primary sources of impurity.
As will be explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 4:2, 5:1.
Who touched vessels that were above the zav and the like. Vessels that were carried over the zav (and other people who defile through lying and sitting), even though he did not touch them.
And they are called madaf. And they are a first degree of impurity, like vessels the zav touched (see Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav UMoshav 6:3).

Even though he is pure for sacred purposes, he became impure regarding the sin offering. Although these vessels do not defile a person regarding sacred purposes (for a first degree of impurity does not defile a person), regarding the sin offering he is impure.
As we have explained. Above, halachah 4.

He touched them with his foot or other part of his body... pure. Since these are a first degree of impurity that does not defile one who touches them with the rest of his body, they did not decree that they defile one pure for the sin offering.
An oven and the like of other vessels. Earthenware vessels, which never become a primary source of impurity (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 10:4).
As will be explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 9:1.
And even amei ha'aretz. Who are generally not believed regarding purities.
Even an earthenware vessel. Which has no purification in a mikveh (Hilchot Mikva'ot 1:3).
And even though that vessel is impure regarding sacred purposes and terumah. For regarding sacred things and terumah an am ha'aretz is not believed (see Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav UMoshav 11:1).

For an earthenware vessel does not become impure from its outer side, even regarding the sin offering. An earthenware vessel is not defiled from its outer side (Hilchot Tumat Met 6:3). And although they instituted extra stringencies for the sin offering, they did not decree that it become impure from its back, for "they never innovated anything regarding the red heifer," and they did not decree impurity on a vessel in a way that it is not fit to become impure at all (Aruch HaShulchan, based on Bavli Chagigah 23b).
As it is said. Regarding the ash of the heifer.
A second-degree food. Food that is a second degree of impurity, whose impurity is from the Torah (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:9).

And the like, of things whose impurity is a light impurity and is Rabbinic. Even if he placed it on something impure by Rabbinic law, such as sacred scriptures (Mishnah Parah 10:3; see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 9:5).
A skylight. An opening in the roof of the house.
In an impure house. That has in it something that defiles by tent.
Opens a handbreadth. An opening of a handbreadth by a handbreadth, which is the measure at which impurity can pass out of the house (see Hilchot Tumat Met 14:1).
If the vessel was of stone. Which does not receive impurity (see Hilchot Tumat Met 6:2).
Whether it has an opening of a handbreadth or not, the ash is pure. And only where the vessel is not lowered into the house (Kesef Mishneh in the name of Rabbi Yosef Korkos).
And enclosed with a tightly bound cover. That has a tight, firmly fitted cover, which saves what is inside it from becoming impure in the tent of a corpse (see Hilchot Tumat Met 20:1).
Foods and liquids of sacred things. For example, flesh of offerings and wine of libations.
But water that is not sanctified. That was filled for the sin offering but not yet sanctified with the ash.

If the owners became impure, the water is disqualified. For when the water is in the domain of impure owners, even though it is enclosed with a tightly bound cover it is considered as if it were in a place that is not pure and is invalid (see Da'at Yosef, Parah 8:1, Ma'arechet 52, and see above 9:17).
On the oven and the like. That do not defile one pure for the sin offering who touches them with his foot (above 13:10).
And stretched out his hand to the window. Where the vessel of waters of the sin offering was placed.
And passed it over the oven. In the air above it.
He is pure. Although the water passed over an impure place, since it was not placed there it is not disqualified.
And likewise a sprinkling that passed over impurity. Waters of the sin offering that during their sprinkling passed over impurity.
if a vessel of the sin-offering became impure. For example, one that is not made of earthenware (see above, halakhah 1).
as we have explained. Above, chapter 13, halakhot 6-7, 10.
for they impart impurity through carrying. They defile the one who carries them not for the purpose of sprinkling (see below 15:1).
because they became impure through the sacred vessel. Since they became impure, lifting them is not for the purpose of sprinkling (Mirkevet ha-Mishneh).
wrapped in paper. For paper does not receive impurity.

even if the sin-offering water was in paper, both are impure. Because the person became impure with regard to the sin-offering through touching a vessel that is not pure for the sin-offering, and he defiles the vessel of the sin-offering through carrying (above 13:5). Once the sin-offering water has become impure, it defiles him in return, making him a first-degree impurity, as with one who carries sin-offering water not for its purpose, and he defiles the sacred vessel.
moved. Shook them without touching them.
as we have explained. Above 13:7.
that it is pure with regard to terumah. Meaning that terumah may be eaten in such a case of doubt.
as will be explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ah 14:1.
and all the doubts about which terumah is left in suspense. One neither eats the terumah nor burns it (see ibid. 13:11).
if they arose with regard to the sin-offering. If the doubt arose concerning sin-offering water.
and if pure foods were prepared on top of those, etc.. That is, they sprinkled from that sin-offering water on vessels and a person, and they later touched pure foods.
and the lattices. Window grates, which are made of wood.
are not like vessels. And they do not receive impurity.
a cake of pressed figs. Figs stuck together.
for all foods... is not pure for the sin-offering. As above 13:1.
and one who eats it is liable to death. At the hands of Heaven, like an impure priest who ate terumah.
and it has already become impure through menstrual waters. For one who is pure for terumah and touches impure menstrual waters becomes impure (below 15:3).
for food does not defile others until it is the size of an egg. Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 4:1.
and it does not defile garments at the time of contact. For regarding one who touches, it does not say "and he shall wash his clothes."
and the impurity of contact with them applies to any amount. Even if he touched a small quantity of sin-offering water, he becomes impure.
if there was enough in them for sprinkling. Water in a quantity from which sprinkling is possible (the measure is explained below).

and one who touches them... defiles garments at the time of contact. Because one who touches the water cannot avoid moving it, he is treated like one who carries it (see Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ah 6:13).
defiles garments at the time of contact or at the time of carrying. He likewise defiles any garment or vessel that touches him while he is in contact with the menstrual waters (above 5:2).
until he separates from the sources of his impurity. As explained there.
all the more so that he should be pure. Therefore the verse cannot be explained according to its plain meaning, but only as he explains in the next paragraph.
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.

the water that is sprinkled at the time of sprinkling... that water is pure. Because dipping the hyssop in the water makes the water on it count as water whose purpose has been fulfilled, which does not defile.
as we have explained. Above 10:9.

for the dipping was for the sake of something that does not receive impurity. But if the dipping was for the sake of something that does receive impurity, the dripping water is considered as having had its purpose fulfilled.
that had water mixed in with them. Above 9:8.
an animal drank from them. Ibid., halakhah 12.
if one pure for terumah touched them he becomes impure. This impurity is rabbinic, since once they have been disqualified they do not defile by Torah law (Kesef Mishneh).

one pure for the sin-offering... remains pure as he was. It seems this is explained as follows: since he is pure for the sin-offering and fit to handle sin-offering water, they did not decree that he become impure because of them (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Parah 9:8: "because they are of the same kind as the thing for which he is pure").
and if one pure for the sin-offering touched them with his hands he becomes impure. As with one who touches other impure liquids (see above 13:10).
that was mixed with ashes of the roasting. Which disqualifies it in any amount (above 9:14).
but they defile through carrying. For one who carries them in any case also carries the ashes of the red heifer.
water not fit to be sanctified. That is, not living water.
and one pure for terumah touched them, etc.. Their law is that of disqualified sin-offering water (above, halakhah 2).
lest he touch the mud and become impure. As above, halakhah 2.

even though it was slaughtered within twenty-four hours. And the water had not yet been digested in it (for if it had eaten the flesh of a corpse, it would defile in such a case; see Hilchot Tum'at Met 20:4).
one who sprinkles, etc.. A person who was sprinkling sin-offering water on the public to purify them.
from the window. Where they would place the sin-offering water (see above 14:5).
and was sprinkled upon. That is, the impure person.
he is exempt. From the variable offering (olah ve-yored) that one who is impure through a corpse brings if he unwittingly entered the Temple (see Hilchot Bi'at ha-Mikdash 3:12).

the people disagreed about the water that drips onto the ground from the window of the public, etc.. Since they sprinkled from it on many people, the ground became wet, and people would slip on the water and get wet, or step on the water with their feet (Commentary to the Mishnah, Parah 12:5).
and enter the Temple. For sin-offering water does not defile after its purpose has been fulfilled.
and they did not worry that perhaps it was disqualified. For then it would defile (above, halakhah 2), since the presumption about water from the public's window is that it is valid.
one who sprinkles with impure hyssop for the sin-offering. For example, one that was gathered for food and was made susceptible to impurity (see above 11:7).
if it has the size of an egg. The measure at which foods defile others (see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 4:1).
the water is valid but the sprinkling is invalid. For a valid sprinkling the hyssop must be pure.
and this hyssop. That has the size of an egg.
for one does not count for a sin-offering. See above 13:6.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1.
